meta.title: Which Italian destinations AI recommends
meta.description: Public observatory of AI visibility in Italian tourism. A hundred territories, two thousand hotels, three assistants. Declared method, open data.

hero.title: Ask an AI where to go in Italy. Five names come out.
hero.lead: Not fifty links to compare: five names, already chosen. We measure which territories make the list, which hotels make the list, and where the AI got its information.
hero.note: Three assistants queried every month, five times per question. Every number is an average, with how much it moved shown next to it.

what.title: What it measures
what.lead: Four things that together make a mark out of 100. Each answers a question a tourism board or a hotelier actually asks.

how.title: How it's built
how.lead: No number comes from a hunch. This is the path every value takes before it reaches the page.

steps.name: The questions
steps.body: Fifty questions per territory, in the two languages Italy gets searched in. Half put the territory in a race with the others in its category, half only check whether the AI knows it.

steps.name: The measurements
steps.body: Every question is asked five times a month to each assistant. The same question gives different answers: one query isn't data, it's an anecdote.

steps.name: The websites
steps.body: For every territory we look at who tells its story and whether AI programs can read them. An AI won't recommend what it was never allowed to read.

steps.name: The number
steps.body: The four factors, weighted, make the score. We publish the average with its spread and the band, because between 38th and 41st place there is no measurable difference.

start.title: Where to start
start.lead: Three doors, depending on what you're after.

paths.name: I have a place in mind
paths.body: Go to its page: score, band, what the AI knows about it, who tells its story, and the twenty hotels we follow there.

paths.name: I want the ranking
paths.body: A hundred territories in order, filterable by assistant. Or one category at a time, which is the comparison that means something.

paths.name: I want to look at hotels
paths.body: Two thousand properties across a hundred territories, with a national ranking and one per territory. The second is the comparison that counts.

paths.name: I want the method
paths.body: The formula, the weights, how many measurements, and the seven things we take for granted before measuring anything.

read.title: How to read a score
read.lead: Three things to know before looking at a number, or you'll read it wrong.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.lead: The things people ask before they even look at a number.

items.q: What is AI visibility for a travel destination?
items.a: It is how often a conversational assistant names that territory when someone asks it where to go, and in which position. Unlike a traditional search, which hands back fifty links to choose from, an AI hands back five names already chosen: either you are in there, or you do not exist.

items.q: Which assistants does the observatory measure?
items.a: Three: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. Each assistant gets its own score alongside the overall one, which is the plain average of the three. No hidden weighting between assistants: if ChatGPT counted more than Perplexity that would be our opinion dressed up as a measurement.

From four weighted factors: comparative presence (how often the territory shows up when it competes with others in its category), internal depth (how much the AI actually knows about the place), cited sources (where it takes its information from) and technical accessibility (whether AI crawlers can read the territory's websites). The formula and the weights are public.

items.q: Why five measurements a month instead of one?
items.a: The same question asked twice of the same model gives two different answers. One question is not data, it is an anecdote. Every month we repeat everything five times per assistant and publish the mean together with how much it moved.

items.q: What does the ± next to the score mean?
items.a: It says how much the answer changed between one run and the next within the same month. The smaller it is, the more reliable the score. It is also why we publish a band rather than just a position: between 38th and 41st place there is no measurable difference.

items.q: Why does it matter whether a destination's website lets crawlers in?
items.a: An AI does not recommend what it could not read. Each assistant sends its crawlers out to read websites: if a territory blocks ChatGPT's, its ChatGPT score drops. This is not technical hygiene, it is visibility.

Yes. No paywall and no sign-up: the rankings are on the page and the same data is downloadable as JSON from the public APIs. The method is stated in full, so anyone can challenge a number knowing how it was produced.

items.q: Are the numbers published right now real measurements?
items.a: Not yet. At this stage the values are generated for demonstration, to build and show the tool, and we say so on every page. They should not be cited as findings. When the real runs begin the banner disappears and the numbers become measured.

open.title: Open data
open.lead: The same numbers you see on the pages, in JSON, no sign-up and no key. If you use them, cite the source.

closing.title: The observatory is public and stays public
closing.body: No paywall, no gated access, method declared. If something about a place you know is wrong, write to us.
